Game Theory

When your best choice depends on what others choose

static games · Nash equilibrium · mixed strategies · oligopoly · timing games · extensive form · subgame perfection · repeated games · auctions · signalling
slides.title: Game Theory

slides.html:
What you will be able to do

  1. Find dominant strategies and Nash equilibria in a payoff matrix
  2. Compute mixed equilibria: when to randomise and with which probabilities
  3. Analyse oligopoly: Cournot, Bertrand, Stackelberg
  4. Use backward induction on sequential games and spot non-credible threats
  5. Handle private information: Bayesian updating, auction bids, signals

The numbers in the examples are small and every step can be done by hand. Proofs can be skipped; in the notes every proof has a one-sentence summary.
slides.title: What you will be able to do
Four kinds of games, four equilibria

slides.html:
Game theory in three sentences

  1. A game = players + strategies + payoffs (plus: who knows what, when)
  2. Equilibrium: given what others do, nobody wants to change alone
  3. Sequential moves require credible threats; private information requires reasonable beliefs

The thread of the course: every extra layer of "order" or "information" adds an equilibrium concept.
slides.title: Game theory in three sentences

slides.html:
1. Decisions and expected utility

First face nature, then face people
slides.title: 1. Decisions and expected utility

slides.html:
An MBA or not?

  • strong demand (prob. \pi): income 100
  • weak demand (1-\pi): income 25
  • no MBA: a sure 49
Attitude MBA if
risk-neutral u=x 25+75\pi\ge49\Rightarrow\pi\ge0.32
risk-averse u=\sqrt x 5+5\pi\ge7\Rightarrow\pi\ge0.4

Expected utility U(P)=\sum_xp(x)u(x). The more curved (concave) u, the more cautious the person.
slides.title: An MBA or not?

slides.html:
2. Dominant strategies

A best choice whatever the others do
slides.title: 2. Dominant strategies

slides.html:
The prisoners' dilemma

Alice \ Bob fink F silent S
F −9, −9 0, −10
S −10, 0 −1, −1
  • Bob finks: Alice compares −9 and −10 → fink
  • Bob is silent: Alice compares 0 and −1 → fink

Finking is dominant; equilibrium (F, F). Yet (S, S) is better for both: individual rationality ≠ collective rationality.
slides.title: The prisoners' dilemma

slides.html:
Same structure, different conclusion

Revenue 30 (cost a^2)

hawk dove
hawk 11, 11 16, 9
dove 9, 16 14, 14

hawk dominant → dilemma

Revenue 12

hawk dove
hawk 2, 2 4, 3
dove 3, 4 5, 5

dove dominant → "delight"

A public good (a street light) is a prisoners' dilemma too: everyone free-rides and the light is never installed.
slides.title: Same structure, different conclusion

slides.html:
Iterated elimination: order matters

c_1 c_2 c_3
r_1 2, 12 1, 10 1, 12
r_2 0, 12 0, 10 0, 11
r_3 0, 12 1, 10 0, 13
  • delete r_3 first → then c_3 → result (r_1,c_1)
  • delete r_2 first → then c_2, c_1 → result (r_1,c_3)

With weakly dominated strategies the order matters; with strictly dominated ones it does not.
slides.title: Iterated elimination: order matters

slides.html:
3. Nash equilibrium

Everyone best-responds to everyone else
slides.title: 3. Nash equilibrium

slides.html:
Definition and the underlining method

u_i(s_i^*,s_{-i}^*)\ge u_i(s_i,s_{-i}^*)\quad\text{for all } i,\ s_i
  • for each column, underline the row player's highest payoff
  • for each row, underline the column player's highest payoff
  • a cell with both payoffs underlined = a pure Nash equilibrium

Nash equilibrium = with the others fixed, nobody gains by changing alone. It does not guarantee a good outcome.
slides.title: Definition and the underlining method

slides.html:
The Battle of the Sexes: two equilibria

Alice \ Bob ballet boxing
ballet 2, 1 0, 0
boxing 0, 0 1, 2
  • two equilibria: (ballet, ballet) and (boxing, boxing)
  • the game itself cannot predict which one occurs
  • if Alice buys tickets first and tells Bob: a first-mover advantage
slides.title: The Battle of the Sexes: two equilibria

slides.html:
Coordination and focal points

Stag hunt

hawk dove
hawk 9, 9 16, 8
dove 8, 16 18, 18

two equilibria, (dove, dove) better

Which side to drive on

left right
left 1, 1 0, 0
right 0, 0 1, 1

UK, Japan left; US, France, Germany right

With several equilibria people coordinate on a focal point: convention, communication, fairness rules, public information. The better equilibrium need not be the less risky one.
slides.title: Coordination and focal points

slides.html:
4. Mixed strategies

Randomise on purpose so the opponent cannot guess
slides.title: 4. Mixed strategies

slides.html:
Matching pennies: no pure equilibrium

Alice \ Bob H T
H 0, 1 1, 0
T 1, 0 0, 1

Alice hides H → Bob guesses H → Alice switches to T → Bob switches to T → … round and round

Just as x^2+1=0 needs complex numbers, games need mixed strategies: a probability for each action.
slides.title: Matching pennies: no pure equilibrium

slides.html:
The key trick: make the opponent indifferent

Mixed equilibrium of the Battle of the Sexes

  • Bob indifferent: 1\cdot p=2(1-p)\Rightarrow p=\tfrac23
  • Alice indifferent: 2q=1-q\Rightarrow q=\tfrac13
  • each expects \tfrac23, less than in either pure equilibrium (they miss each other with prob. \tfrac59)

My probabilities are pinned down by the opponent's payoffs.
slides.title: The key trick: make the opponent indifferent
Three equilibria of the Battle of the Sexes

slides.html:
The inspection game

Firm \ Agency inspect trust
pollute 4-F, 5-C 4, 0
clean 3, 5-C 3, 5
  • firm indifferent: 4-qF=3\Rightarrow q^*=1/F
  • agency indifferent: 5-C=5(1-p)\Rightarrow p^*=C/5
  • e.g. F=4, C=2 → inspect \tfrac14, pollute \tfrac25

A higher fine does not lower the pollution probability, only the inspection rate.
slides.title: The inspection game

slides.html:
The value of commitment

  • announce first: announce "inspect", the firm cleans up, pollution probability 0
  • many firms: announcing an inspection rate \theta=1/F makes every firm clean up
3\ge4-\theta F\iff\theta\ge\frac1F,\qquad\text{agency gets }5-\frac CF>5-C

Committing to an inspection rate beats randomising on the spot: the logic of random spot checks.
slides.title: The value of commitment

slides.html:
Existence (Advanced)

  • Theorem: strategy sets nonempty, compact, convex, payoffs continuous and quasi-concave in own strategy ⇒ a Nash equilibrium exists
  • pure strategies \{0,1\} are not convex → matching pennies has no pure equilibrium
  • with mixing the strategy set is a segment and payoffs are linear → existence

Every finite game has a (possibly mixed) Nash equilibrium.
slides.title: Existence (Advanced)

slides.html:
5. Oligopoly

Benchmark: P=13-Q, cost c=1
slides.title: 5. Oligopoly

slides.html:
Bertrand: simultaneous prices

  • price above cost → the rival cuts a little and takes the whole market
  • prices fall all the way to p_1=p_2=c=1, profits 0
  • Bertrand paradox: two firms give the perfectly competitive outcome

It relies on three assumptions: identical products, identical costs, unlimited capacity (relaxed in Chapter 6).
slides.title: Bertrand: simultaneous prices

slides.html:
Cournot: simultaneous quantities

\max_{q_1}(13-q_1-q_2-1)q_1\ \Rightarrow\ q_1=6-\frac{q_2}2
  • symmetric solution q=6-q/2\Rightarrow q^*=4, P=5, profit 16 each
  • colluding at 3 each gives 18 each, but if the rival makes 3 I want 4.5 and get 20.25

Cournot is a prisoners' dilemma too: everyone wants to secretly produce more.
slides.title: Cournot: simultaneous quantities

slides.html:
Stackelberg: sequential quantities

  1. follower: q_2=6-q_1/2
  2. the leader plugs it in: \max_{q_1}\frac{(12-q_1)q_1}2\Rightarrow q_1=6
  3. q_2=3, P=4, profits 18 vs 9

In quantity competition moving first pays: the leader grabs a large output.
slides.title: Stackelberg: sequential quantities

slides.html:
Differentiated products: price competition

q_1=150-p_1+p_2, q_2=100-p_2+p_1, cost 50

  • p_1=100+p_2/2, p_2=75+p_1/2
  • equilibrium p_1\approx183.3, p_2\approx166.7, profits about 17 778 and 13 611
  • price leadership: p_1=250, p_2=200, profits 20 000 vs 22 500

In price competition moving second pays: the follower just undercuts a little and takes sales.
slides.title: Differentiated products: price competition

slides.html:
6. Escaping the Bertrand paradox

product differences · cost differences · capacity limits
slides.title: 6. Escaping the Bertrand paradox

slides.html:
Asymmetric costs and capacity limits

  • asymmetric costs c_1>c_2: firm 2 prices just below c_1 and earns (a-c_1)(c_1-c_2)
    • e.g. a=10, c_1=4, c_2=2 → profit 12
  • limited capacity: if the rival raises its price, consumers who miss the cheap goods must buy from it → p=c is no longer an equilibrium
  • capacity first, then prices = Cournot: k_i=\frac{a-1}3

Break any of the three assumptions and the price stays above cost.
slides.title: Asymmetric costs and capacity limits

slides.html:
7. Timing games

Not how much, but when
slides.title: 7. Timing games
Preemption: the first-mover advantage is used up

slides.html:
Product races and the war of attrition

Product race

  • both launch together, p_1(t^*)+p_2(t^*)=1
  • e.g. t/10+t/15=1\Rightarrow t^*=6
  • leader's winning chance 0.6 = follower's 0.6

War of attrition (prize v, cost 1 per period)

  • indifference: (1-p)v-p=0
  • p^*=\frac v{v+1}; with v=3 fight with prob. \tfrac34
  • expected value 0: the prize is burnt
slides.title: Product races and the war of attrition

slides.html:
8. Information structure

Who knows what, and when
slides.title: 8. Information structure

slides.html:
Sequential moves: strategy = complete plan

Bob chooses after seeing Alice's choice; he has 4 strategies: follow, opposite, always DVD, always Blu-ray.

Alice \ Bob follow opposite always D always BR
DVD 1, 1 −1, −1 1, 1 −1, −1
Blu-ray 3, 3 −1, −1 −1, −1 3, 3

3 Nash equilibria; (DVD, always DVD) rests on a non-credible threat.
slides.title: Sequential moves: strategy = complete plan

slides.html:
Bayesian games

  • Harsanyi: nature first draws each player's type; each sees only his own
  • strategy = a function from types to actions
  • Bayesian Nash equilibrium: every type best-responds in expectation

Three-step check: propose strategies → compute beliefs by Bayes' rule → verify optimality

P(k\mid B)=\frac{P(B\mid k)P(k)}{\sum_jP(B\mid j)P(j)}
slides.title: Bayesian games

slides.html:
Example: Bob is unsure of the payoffs

  • prior 0.6, 0.3, 0.1; candidate: Alice picks Blu-ray in cases 1, 3 and DVD in case 2; Bob follows
  • after Blu-ray: P(1\mid B)=\frac{0.6}{0.7}=\frac67, P(3\mid B)=\frac17
  • Bob: Blu-ray \frac{20}7 > DVD -\frac57 ✓
  • after DVD: surely case 2, DVD gives 4 ✓

Beliefs depend on equilibrium strategies, so: guess the equilibrium, compute beliefs, then verify.
slides.title: Example: Bob is unsure of the payoffs

slides.html:
9. Subgame perfection

Threats must be credible
slides.title: 9. Subgame perfection

slides.html:
Subgame perfect equilibrium

  • subgame: a branch starting at a single-node information set that cuts no information set
  • SPE: a Nash equilibrium in every subgame
  • removes Nash equilibria that rely on non-credible threats off the path

Backward induction (Kuhn: finite perfect-information games always have an SPE)

  1. start at the last move and let the mover pick his best option
  2. prune: replace the node by the payoffs
  3. repeat up to the root
slides.title: Subgame perfect equilibrium

slides.html:
The takeover game

  • share price 100, worth 110 after a takeover; the investor bids b
  • the firm accepts ⟺ b-100\ge100-b ⟺ b\ge100
  • the investor gets 110-b, so she bids b=100 and gains 10 per share

Solve the last mover first, then let earlier movers anticipate later reactions.
slides.title: The takeover game

slides.html:
The monitoring game

  • no-monitoring subgame: a low wage is dominant for the employer → low effort → employer gets 20
  • monitoring subgame: high effort (30-e>10) → employer gets 60-m
  • m<20 → monitor. Unique SPE: monitor, high effort

Behaviour strategies (Advanced): when a subgame has only a mixed equilibrium, the SPE randomises separately at each information set.
slides.title: The monitoring game

slides.html:
10. Repeated games

How long relationships sustain cooperation
slides.title: 10. Repeated games

slides.html:
Finite repetition

  • repeating a stage equilibrium every period is always an SPE
  • unique stage equilibrium ⇒ the unique SPE of finite repetition plays it every period (reason back from the last period)
  • one-shot deviation principle: only check "deviate in one period"

Two stage equilibria allow cooperation: (H, H) in period 1; (M, M) next if kept, else (L, L)

10+2\delta\le8+6\delta\iff\delta\ge\tfrac12
slides.title: Finite repetition

slides.html:
A Cournot cartel

  • collude at 3 each, earning 18; deviate to 4.5, earning 20.25 once; then Cournot 16 each
\frac{18}{1-\delta}\ge20.25+\frac{16\delta}{1-\delta}\iff\delta\ge\frac9{17}\approx0.53

The threshold does not depend on a,c: all three profits are proportional to (a-c)^2.
slides.title: A Cournot cartel

slides.html:
Carrot and stick

L R
U 4, 4 2, 5
D 5, 1 1, 2
  • normally play (U, L); after a deviation → one period of (D, R) → back to (U, L)
  • player 1: \delta\ge\frac13; player 2: 5+2\delta\le4+4\delta\Rightarrow\delta\ge\frac12

Short and credible punishment: accepting it is the only way back to cooperation.
slides.title: Carrot and stick

slides.html:
11. Auctions and mechanism design

Bidding with private information
slides.title: 11. Auctions and mechanism design

slides.html:
Second-price auctions: bid your value

  • your bid only decides whether you win, not what you pay
  • bid low: you may miss a profitable deal; bid high: you may win and lose money
  • e.g. values 10, 7, 4 → the bidder with 10 wins, pays 7, gains 3

Bidding your value is weakly dominant. The English auction is equivalent.
slides.title: Second-price auctions: bid your value

slides.html:
Revenue equivalence

Two bidders, values uniform on [0,1]:

  • first price: E[\tfrac12\max]=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac23=\tfrac13
  • second price: E[\min]=1-\tfrac23=\tfrac13

Symmetric independent private values, highest value wins, zero value pays zero ⇒ every auction gives the same expected revenue.
slides.title: Revenue equivalence

slides.html:
The revelation principle

  • selling mechanism: messages, probabilities of getting the item, payments
  • direct mechanism: the message = a report of one's value
  • incentive compatible: truthful reporting is an equilibrium

The equilibrium outcome of any mechanism can be reached by an incentive-compatible direct mechanism. A designer only needs to consider rules under which people tell the truth.
slides.title: The revelation principle

slides.html:
12. Perfect Bayesian equilibrium and signalling

Actions themselves carry information
slides.title: 12. Perfect Bayesian equilibrium and signalling

slides.html:
The market for lemons

  • the seller knows the car's quality, the buyer does not; half good, half bad
  • low price seen: surely a bad car, buy
  • high price seen: belief still half-half, buy ⟺ \frac{b_h+b_l}2\ge s_h

Example: b_h=10, s_h=8, b_l=4: 7<8 → good cars leave, only lemons remain

This game has no proper subgame, so SPE does not help: we need beliefs.
slides.title: The market for lemons

slides.html:
Perfect Bayesian equilibrium

  1. sequential rationality: at every information set, actions are optimal given beliefs
  2. consistent beliefs: Bayes' rule on the path; off the path, as consistent with equilibrium strategies as possible

Example: (r, L, L′) is a Nash equilibrium, but L is dominant for player 2, so player 3 must believe \mu(D)=1, and then L′ is not optimal → not a PBE
slides.title: Perfect Bayesian equilibrium

slides.html:
A signalling game: check all four cases

type (L,u) (L,d) (R,u) (R,d)
t_1 1, 3 4, 0 2, 1 0, 0
t_2 2, 4 0, 1 1, 0 1, 2
  • pool on L: a(L)=u, need a(R)=d, i.e. \mu'\le\frac23 ✓
  • pool on R: t_1 deviates to L ✗
  • t_1→L, t_2→R: t_2 mimics t_1 ✗
  • t_1→R, t_2→L: (u,u), nobody deviates ✓
slides.title: A signalling game: check all four cases

slides.title: Summary

slides.html:
One storyline

Kind of game Equilibrium What it adds
static, complete info Nash everyone best-responds
static, mixing mixed make the opponent indifferent
dynamic, complete info subgame perfect credible threats
static, incomplete info Bayesian Nash every type optimal in expectation
dynamic, incomplete info perfect Bayesian beliefs consistent with strategies

individual ≠ collective rationality · rule details decide outcomes · commitment must be credible · long relationships sustain cooperation · information is costly
slides.title: One storyline

slides.html:
Common misconceptions

  • ✗ A Nash equilibrium is the best outcome → it only means nobody wants to change alone
  • ✗ Mixing probabilities depend on my own payoffs → on the opponent's payoffs
  • ✗ Moving first always helps → in price competition moving second is better
  • ✗ Announcing a threat is enough → it must be one you would carry out
  • ✗ Repetition always brings cooperation → not with a unique stage equilibrium and finite repetition
  • ✗ First-price auctions raise more → revenue equivalence
  • ✗ Education pays only because it raises productivity → signals can pay too
slides.title: Common misconceptions
